To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the binding of human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to its receptors is accompanied by a change in the accessibility of a receptor-bound epitope, suggesting a role for receptor oligomerization in the transduction of the cytokine signal.

a monoclonal antibody directed against an exposed epitope of the hGCSF (8C2) inhibits the proliferative response of a human myeloid leucemia cell line induced by hGCSF, whereas another antibody that recognizes a buried epitope (6E3) does not.
a temperature-induced receptor oligomerisation process is responsible for the masking of an epitope in the human granulocyt-colony stimulating factor:receptor complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural changes occurring in cytokine-receptor complexes, which may be important for the understanding of the molecular mechanism of signal transduction.
the study of the role of epitopes of hG-CSF in the receptor-mediated proliferative signal.
the accessibility of epitopes in cytokine:receptors complexes and the role of these epitopes in signal transduction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the epitope 8c2 is not involved in signal transduction.
the accessibility of epitope 6E3 remains constant during the whole process of hG-CSF-receptor binding and internalization, whereas epitope 8c2 becomes masked after the ligand-receptor interaction.
the accessibility of the 8C2 region in the hG-CS-F molecule depends on the binding to its receptor, but also on the state of aggregation of the receptor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the epitope 8-C2, that is located in the hG-CSFR region 1, is masked by the hG-CSR region 2, when the hG-CSFr is oligomerized.
the accessibility of the epitope 8 C2 is a good indicator of the receptor aggregation and, consequently, of the signal transduction.
the epitope 8c2 is exposed in the hG-CSf:receptor complexes formed in vitro and is accessible to mAb 8c2 in the hGCSF:receptor complexes present on the cell surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the binding of a monoclonal antibody to the hG-CSFR can induce a conformational change in the receptor that masks an epitope on hG-CSF.
a receptor oligomeric state is required for signal transduction, but the exact mechanism is not clear.
the accessibility of epitope 2C8 is changed when G-CSF is bound to the receptor.
